messages.author: 4599a1b66e2bbbb0
messages.subject: fluctuations ~ missing data
parts:
Hi all, 

i am posting here a figure of the mean densities (hares/100ha) from 1995 to 2021 (in autumn to 2020) in spring (turquoise) and autumn (orange). Large dots illustrate densities estimated with the year-stratified N-mix. Black lines show the densities estimated with pcount in unmarked for each year individually. The numbers below the curves indicate the number of sites in the respective years. In total, the site x year matrix contains 144 sites, i.e. new sites entered the monitoring scheme while others no longer provided any data.
 
What I find suspicious is that the trend lines show little fluctuation over the period when most areas provided data (i.e. from 2005 to 2010). The question to me is, if the observed fluctuations in the years with few or falling numbers of sites with data can be attributed to the absence of important sites or if the match of the smooth part of the curves with higher number of sites with data is pure chance, so that the problem can actually be neglected because the dynamic N-mix compensates for missing data?

Has anyone experienced similar patterns and knows about the influence of missing data relative to the population and detection process?

Very best,
Tobias.

messages.author: 39971e2c19b8ec70
messages.subject: Re: fluctuations ~ missing data
parts:
Hello,

you can look at the width of the CIs in different years. You probably don't have a large sample enough (of years) to test if e.g. variance in certain time periods differs significantly. 

To my eye, it looks like the fluctuation can be caused by the number of sites, because you can see that the CIs in 2005-2010 are very small, less than half of the others. But some of the fluctuations are can not only be attributed to CIs; it could be changes in sites as you suggest, or, just some years were more fluctuating than others - this is hard to tell, because you have only six year sample in those stable years 2005-2010, so it could just happen that the population was more stable there than in other years.

What you could do is to look at the variance of density among sites in different years and make similar plot of that (maybe do a boxplot to see the outliers as well?). This could help you see whether the change in monitored sites could have had big impact or not. You can then check if the sites which appeared/disappeared were among the outliers.

Tomas

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: fluctuations ~ missing data
parts:
Dear Tobi, hello Tomas,

couple of random comments:
  • I don't have a bad feeling when looking at this plot. I agree that the greater fluctuations of the point estimates in the early and the late years could be a simple sample size effect: the (much) smaller number of sites on which the estimates then are based is reflected in the wider CRIs, but may also lead to more "wobbly" point estimates.
  • Another thing to check may be the magnitude of preferential sampling in the data set. Perhaps in the early and the late years contain counts from sites that are somehow different than those in the middle years, for instance, from smaller areas, which may have larger fluctuations ?
  • I am interested to see that the presumably simpler model with pcount in unmarked produced a consistently smaller estimate than the model for all years together. Presumably this is because there is more unmodelled heterogeneity in the analysis with unmarked, and this leads to a slight negative bias of the estimates ?
  • Perhaps the coollest analysis might be a dynamic version of the Nmix model, i.e., the fitting of a Dail-Madsen model to the twice-per-year counts. That is, you'd express the expected density in, say, spring as the expected density in the previous autumn, times a population growth rate. Of course, you'd have to estimate a separate growth rate for the two types of transitions (spring to autumn and autumn to spring), because the former contains reproduction and the latter only survival and dispersal. Such a model with temporal autocorrelation would also smooth the series somewhat.
Best regards  ----- Marc

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Effects of unmarked abundance heterogeneity in the Nmix model (an Erratum to AHM1)
parts:
Dear all,

unfortunately the Google version of the AHM book website (https://sites.google.com/site/appliedhierarchicalmodeling/errata) has been blocked for editing for more than a year now. We don't understand why and have long felt we should re-create this website elsewhere .... but haven't had the time so far.

In the meantime I felt we owe you the record of at least one error that Andy discovered recently in the chapter on binomial Nmix models in AHM1. In its Section 6.7 we present a simulation-based study of the effects of assumption violations in the static Nmix model. Most of these have to do with unmodelled heterogeneity of some kind; results are summarized in Table 6.2 on p. 249. 

The first type of unmodelled heterogeneity examined concerns that at the site level in abundance. We simulated data with the following settings of the simNmix() function:
simNmix(... mean.lam = exp(1), sigma.lam = 1, .... )

The heterogeneity-naive model produces a point estimate of 4.04, and we compare this with a true value that we claim is 2.71 (i.e., exp(1)). But this is WRONG, since the expected value of a log-normal distribution is the mean plus 0.5 times the variance (you can check this out on Wikipedia). Hence, the proper benchmark for truth is exp(1.5) = 4.48. Thus, we conclude that unmodelled site-level heterogeneity in abundance leads to an underestimate of abundance, and not to an overestimate as we erroneously state in the book.

The other comparisons with abundance should be OK, though.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: 4599a1b66e2bbbb0
messages.subject: Re: fluctuations ~ missing data
parts:
Dear Tomas and Marc,

thanks a lot for your thoughts and comments. 
I checked the variances in density of the first count in the raw data. The plot is based on a one-way ANOVA with year as fixed (blue) and random (red) effect (Bayesian shrinkage as in the Blue bugs book).

According to this, there is not much change in the variances. Also preferential sampling should not be an issue. Though there were no areas smaller than ~ 200ha before 2003, variance in sampling area did not change during the period of interest (2004 - today):

Meanwhile, i did another analysis, successively reducing the amount of sites from at least 1 year with data (the original dataset) to sites with at least 10 years with data, thereby reducing the amount of data in the "middle years" and thus the discrepancy between 2004-2010 (now max 60 sites) and the following years (~30 sites with data). The resulting plot (bigger points = more years with data = less total sites) shows that there is much confidence that the trend is due to the population process and not due to patterns in the data, so i think your feeling was right :-).


Interestingly, the curves start to "converge" around 2002, which was the year when the coordinated monitoring scheme started. Also, the smooth part between 2004 and 2010 is less obvious now. @Marc: i will give a try to fitting a Dail-Madsen model to the twice-per-year counts as soon as i return from my holidays. Would you also suggest fitting a C[i,j,k,t] - N-mix with k=season as outlined in 2.3.2 of your AHM2 - book?

Thanks again & best regards,

Tobias.

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: fluctuations ~ missing data
parts:
Dear Tobias,

these are interesting patterns, thanks.

About a possible "seasonal" DM fit to your data. No, the model in 2.3.2 in AHM2 is not a "dynamic" model, but a "static", where change in the system is modelled by simply making parameters year-dependent (what we call "year-stratified"). In contrast, a dynamic model has some sort of autoregression, where the state at some time t+1 depends in some way (i.e., as estimated by some parameter) on the state at time t.

If you want to fit a DM model to your data you ought to string out your into a 3d array C[i,j,t], where t denotes the season, which runs from 1 to about 56 (the latter being the number of years times 2). I think this would be a quite cool analysis.

Best regards -- Marc

Hello,

you can look at the width of the CIs in different years. You probably don't have a large sample enough (of years) to test if e.g. variance in certain time periods differs significantly. 

To my eye, it looks like the fluctuation can be caused by the number of sites, because you can see that the CIs in 2005-2010 are very small, less than half of the others. But some of the fluctuations are can not only be attributed to CIs; it could be changes in sites as you suggest, or, just some years were more fluctuating than others - this is hard to tell, because you have only six year sample in those stable years 2005-2010, so it could just happen that the population was more stable there than in other years.

What you could do is to look at the variance of density among sites in different years and make similar plot of that (maybe do a boxplot to see the outliers as well?). This could help you see whether the change in monitored sites could have had big impact or not. You can then check if the sites which appeared/disappeared were among the outliers.

Tomas

messages.subject: Erratum
parts:
Thanks Marc for your suggestions,

meanwhile, i found out that in the analysis, where i successively reduced the amount of sites from at least 1 year with data (the original dataset) to only sites with at least 10 years with data, i did not correctly allocate the taxation areas. This resulted in the scatter before 2002. I corrected these and now the trends in density are virtually the same, regardless of the number of sites between 2005 and 2010 is ~100 (>= 1 year with data, red curve in the fig. below) or ~60 (>=10 years with data, light brown curves in fig. below). The removal of sites with few data tended to increase estimated hare density slightly between 2005 and 2010.
Fig. mean hare densities in autumn from 1994 to 2020. Light brown points depict estimated densities successively removing sites with at least 1 to 9 years of data. Red points show the density with the full dataset (>=1 year with data). Patterns in spring densities estimations with different amount of data are similar.

Best regards,
Tobias.

On Saturday, August 6, 2022 at 3:07:36 PM UTC+2 marc.kery wrote:
Dear Tobias,

these are interesting patterns, thanks.

About a possible "seasonal" DM fit to your data. No, the model in 2.3.2 in AHM2 is not a "dynamic" model, but a "static", where change in the system is modelled by simply making parameters year-dependent (what we call "year-stratified"). In contrast, a dynamic model has some sort of autoregression, where the state at some time t+1 depends in some way (i.e., as estimated by some parameter) on the state at time t.

If you want to fit a DM model to your data you ought to string out your into a 3d array C[i,j,t], where t denotes the season, which runs from 1 to about 56 (the latter being the number of years times 2). I think this would be a quite cool analysis.

Best regards -- Marc



From: hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Tobi Lu <tob...@web.de>
Sent: Friday, August 5, 2022 11:25
To: hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology <hmec...@googlegroups.com>

Subject: Re: fluctuations ~ missing data
Dear Tomas and Marc,

thanks a lot for your thoughts and comments. 
I checked the variances in density of the first count in the raw data. The plot is based on a one-way ANOVA with year as fixed (blue) and random (red) effect (Bayesian shrinkage as in the Blue bugs book).

According to this, there is not much change in the variances. Also preferential sampling should not be an issue. Though there were no areas smaller than ~ 200ha before 2003, variance in sampling area did not change during the period of interest (2004 - today):

Meanwhile, i did another analysis, successively reducing the amount of sites from at least 1 year with data (the original dataset) to sites with at least 10 years with data, thereby reducing the amount of data in the "middle years" and thus the discrepancy between 2004-2010 (now max 60 sites) and the following years (~30 sites with data). The resulting plot (bigger points = more years with data = less total sites) shows that there is much confidence that the trend is due to the population process and not due to patterns in the data, so i think your feeling was right :-).


Interestingly, the curves start to "converge" around 2002, which was the year when the coordinated monitoring scheme started. Also, the smooth part between 2004 and 2010 is less obvious now. @Marc: i will give a try to fitting a Dail-Madsen model to the twice-per-year counts as soon as i return from my holidays. Would you also suggest fitting a C[i,j,k,t] - N-mix with k=season as outlined in 2.3.2 of your AHM2 - book?

Thanks again & best regards,

Tobias.


On Wednesday, August 3, 2022 at 10:50:24 AM UTC+2 marc.kery wrote:
Dear Tobi, hello Tomas,

couple of random comments:
  • I don't have a bad feeling when looking at this plot. I agree that the greater fluctuations of the point estimates in the early and the late years could be a simple sample size effect: the (much) smaller number of sites on which the estimates then are based is reflected in the wider CRIs, but may also lead to more "wobbly" point estimates.
  • Another thing to check may be the magnitude of preferential sampling in the data set. Perhaps in the early and the late years contain counts from sites that are somehow different than those in the middle years, for instance, from smaller areas, which may have larger fluctuations ?
  • I am interested to see that the presumably simpler model with pcount in unmarked produced a consistently smaller estimate than the model for all years together. Presumably this is because there is more unmodelled heterogeneity in the analysis with unmarked, and this leads to a slight negative bias of the estimates ?
  • Perhaps the coollest analysis might be a dynamic version of the Nmix model, i.e., the fitting of a Dail-Madsen model to the twice-per-year counts. That is, you'd express the expected density in, say, spring as the expected density in the previous autumn, times a population growth rate. Of course, you'd have to estimate a separate growth rate for the two types of transitions (spring to autumn and autumn to spring), because the former contains reproduction and the latter only survival and dispersal. Such a model with temporal autocorrelation would also smooth the series somewhat.
Best regards  ----- Marc

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: Erratum
parts:
Dear Tobi,

thanks for the additional info. What you did is a sort of sensitivity analysis: you have a component in your model about which you are a little unsure ... and it's hard or impossible to test which choice of that component is the "right" one. So you vary that component randomly to see how sensitive (=changeable) your main inferences of interest are. If they don't change much, then that's fine and the choice doesn't matter so much. If the inferences do change, then that doesn't mean that your model is wrong ... but perhaps that you have to do some more thinking. And explaining for the reviewers 🙂

Other examples of sensitivity analysis are for the choice of priors in a model fit in the Bayesian way or the choice of fixed parameter in a population model where you may not have information about some process (such as juvenile survival perhaps).

Best regards  --- Marc
